1.pericope_label: Boast not thyself of tomorrow: let another man praise thee: a fool’s wrath is heavier than stone and sand: open rebuke is better than secret love

schools.summary: Henry distinguishes presuming upon tomorrow from preparing for it and turns the caution on the delay of conversion, observes that everyone is forward to run down the man who cries himself up, gives the rule of getting out of a fool’s way while his passion lasts, illustrates settled envy by the javelin David escaped, and answers the fifth verse with the maxim that the physician’s care is to cure the disease and not to please the palate.

Gill answers the first verse with images of the grass, the flower and the declining shadow rather than argument, allows the exception that a man may commend himself when the glory of God or self-vindication requires it, names the outrages of wrath in the brothers at Shechem, the king of the bondage and the murderer of the infants, and holds against an interpreter he cites that reproof among friends should be given privately.

Clarke notes that every man wishes for tomorrow and wishes for it again when it comes, derives our word morning from the reading of an old English manuscript, matches the Latin saying about self-praise with an English one, tells the rabbinic story of the envious man who asked to lose an eye so that his neighbour might lose both, and illustrates open rebuke by the man whose enemy opened an abscess and saved his life; Wesley defines the secret love as one that never shows itself in free and faithful reproof.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the particle of boasting and the accents of the first verse, take the stone and sand as genitives so that the fool’s wrath is heavier for those it falls on, quote a Jewish proverb that a man is known by his wine-glass, his purse and his anger, narrow the jealousy of the fourth verse against a scholar who generalised it to enmity, and refuse on grammatical grounds the reading that makes the secret love a love which conceals a friend’s faults; Ellicott traces boasting and anxiety alike to too much dependence upon self and holds that wrath subsides like a storm while jealousy never can be set at rest.

debates: What is the secret love of the fifth verse? Keil and Delitzsch reject the common reading, in which it is a love that from false indulgence keeps a friend’s faults concealed, since the grammar would require another form, and reject an attempt to accommodate the text to that sense; their own reading is that stern correction from anyone, foe or friend, is better than being the object of such a love. Ellicott and Wesley take it as a love that never discloses itself in acts of kindness or in reproof, and Gill reports an interpreter who makes the rebuke public before ruling that reproof among friends should be private.
outliers: Clarke turns aside from the first verse to etymology, deriving our word morning from an old English manuscript rendering that means a continuance of time to dwell in.
Keil and Delitzsch quote a Jewish proverb that a man is known by three things whose names sound alike, his wine-glass, his purse and his anger.
Gill alone allows an exception to the rule against self-praise, when the glory of God, the credit of religion or self-vindication requires a man to speak for himself.
Clarke answers the question about envy with a rabbinic tale in which the envious man, offered anything on condition that his neighbour receive double, asks to lose one eye.
themes: presuming on tomorrow, not preparing for it
self-praise that defiles the mouth
a storm that subsides and a fire that does not
a man known by his purse and his anger
the physician who does not please the palate

6.pericope_label: Faithful are the wounds of a friend: the full soul loatheth an honeycomb: as a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place

schools.summary: Henry gives the English proverb that hunger is the best sauce, observes that those who fare sumptuously nauseate delicate food as a people once did the quails while the hungry bless God for bread and water, holds that a man’s place is his castle so that those who love to be abroad leave their work at home undone, and allows that a friend need not be a relation, since a friend is distinguished from a brother throughout the book.

Gill takes the wounds for reproofs that grieve for the present but proceed from love, applies the loathed honeycomb to the man full of his own wisdom and righteousness to whom the Gospel is insipid, is careful that the oil of the ninth verse is not the holy anointing oil but the common sort poured on guests, and illustrates the old friend from the royal house, the father who valued his ally and the son who forsook the old men and lost ten tribes.

Clarke reads the wandering bird as emigration and says he has seen multitudes of such wanderers come to great misery, describes at first hand the fumigating of guests’ beards and the sprinkling of rose-water, with two silver-inlaid vessels before him as he writes, and advises that in adversity a man apply to an old family friend rather than to the nearest relative who keeps his distance; Wesley glosses the kisses as the whole outward profession of friendship and the wandering as vanity and lightness.

Keil and Delitzsch reject two derivations of the word for the enemy’s kisses and decline to load a fourth meaning on a word that already carries three, give the German proverb that hunger is the best cook and warn that self-contentment is the worst poverty, insist that the wandering of the eighth verse is an unwilling flight rather than needless roaming, reject a Greek reading that makes the ninth verse speak of a soul torn by calamities, and call an inherited friend a family heirloom; Ellicott renders the kisses plentiful rather than deceitful and holds that in spiritual things the less we content ourselves with the less hunger we feel.

debates: What is the wandering of the eighth verse? Clarke takes it for emigration in search of a better living, and reports that he has seen many such wanderers come to misery. Ellicott takes it for exile, a man who has lost his home rather than left it, and Keil and Delitzsch agree, insisting on an unwilling flight and setting aside a scholar who read the verse as a warning against needless roaming supported by an Arabic proverb that journeying is a part of the pains of hell. Henry keeps a moral sense, of men who do not know when they are well off and leave their work at home undone.
outliers: Ellicott inverts the proverb of the seventh verse for the soul, holding that in spiritual things the less a man contents himself with, the less hunger he feels and the less enjoyment he derives.
Keil and Delitzsch decline a proposed etymology on the ground that the Hebrew word already has three meanings and should not be loaded with a fourth invented for this passage.
Clarke describes the perfuming of guests from his own experience, with two silver-inlaid vessels of some quarts each standing before him as he writes.
Keil and Delitzsch describe a friend inherited from a father as a family heirloom descending from father to son.
themes: kisses plentiful rather than false
hunger as the best sauce and the best cook
a flight, not an excursion
beards perfumed at the end of a feast
a friendship inherited like an heirloom

11.pericope_label: My son, be wise, and make my heart glad: a prudent man foreseeth the evil: he that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, it shall be counted a curse to him

schools.summary: Henry supplies the reproach the father means to answer, that he was over-strict in keeping his children from the liberties others take, and the taunt that a young saint makes an old devil; holds that an honest man may be made a beggar but is not honest who makes himself one, and that foolish lending is an injustice to our families; and finds in the early rising of the fourteenth verse a reason the others miss, that the morning is the time when God is to be praised.

Gill takes the evil foreseen in the twelfth verse first as the evil of sin, seen in the defacing of the image of God, and then as the evil of punishment, and describes the flatterer of the fourteenth verse as a man who exceeds all bounds of modesty and truth with pompous words and hyperbolical expressions.

Clarke disposes of the two repeated verses with cross-references and answers the loud blessing with an Italian proverb, that he who praises you more than he was wont has either deceived you or is about to do it; Wesley makes the reproach of the eleventh verse the reproach of being the father of a wicked son, and states of the fourteenth that the friend will value such a blessing no more than a curse.

Keil and Delitzsch prefer become wise to be wise, quote a commentator’s version of what such a father has to hear, discuss the accents of the twelfth verse and hold that the conditional reading tenable at its earlier occurrence will not do here, note that the word for prudent alliterates with the word for surety, take the strange thing pledged for as a matter rather than a woman, and observe that the fourteenth verse reaches back over three intervening proverbs to the ones on friendship; Ellicott takes the eleventh verse as the address of a father or master and pictures the bystanders whose attention the flatterer draws upon his patron.

debates: Is the loud blessing merely tactless or is it calculated? Keil and Delitzsch make the heaviness of the first line deliberate, a portrait of a man calling out good wishes to give the impression of deep veneration while in fact bidding for favour, the mark of a selfish and servile soul. Henry agrees that praising men is a way of getting more out of them, and adds that the early rising takes from God praise that is his alone. Ellicott is gentler, treating the man chiefly as a nuisance whose noise embarrasses his patron before the bystanders.
outliers: Henry finds in the rising early a reason none of the others give, that the morning belongs to the praise of God and should not be spent praising a friend.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the fourteenth verse reaches back over the three intervening proverbs to the ones on friendship, and that the verses on prudence and suretyship stand together because their opening words alliterate.
Clarke answers the proverb with a proverb, the Italian saying that a man who praises you more than he was wont has either deceived you or is about to do it.
Henry rules out the obvious remedy for a bad surety, since a man who makes himself a common voucher will produce sureties as insolvent as himself.
themes: become wise, not be wise
a father answering his critics
a conditional reading refused
a compliment paid at daybreak
praise that expects to be paid

15.pericope_label: A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike: iron sharpeneth iron: as in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man

schools.summary: Henry distinguishes a neighbour’s contentions, which are a sharp shower one may shelter from, from a wife’s, which are a constant soaking rain; holds that one man is nobody and that poring upon a book in a corner will not accomplish a man as the studying of men will, while warning that bad company sharpens the passions as good company sharpens the graces; encourages the gardener and the servant alike in mean employments; and divides the last verse into a way of knowing ourselves and a way of knowing others by ourselves.

Gill observes that wind pent up makes the greater noise, and so does the contentious woman for all the methods used to still her; explains the sharpening from the butcher whetting his knife; and cites a Latin author for the observation that all things appear greater through water.

Clarke admits the Hebrew of the sixteenth verse is very obscure and quotes an old English version for it, asks whether a Latin poet had seen the seventeenth verse in the Greek when he wrote of serving as the hone that gives edge to razors, and quotes a verse to the effect that if each man saw another’s heart there would be no commerce; Wesley notes that the right hand spreads the savour of ointment by its much stirring, and makes the likeness of hearts in the last verse their agreement in the corruption of nature.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the fifteenth and sixteenth verses as one four-line proverb and prefer to derive the word for the rainy day from unbroken continuousness rather than from the shutting up of people indoors, reject a translation of the seventeenth verse that turns it into two exclamations, report why the fig tree is the apt figure since it needs years of training before it bears, and object that the particle of the nineteenth verse is a preposition and cannot govern a clause; Ellicott has the woman slipping through the hand like oil, the play of wit brightening the face, and the merciful and the evil each recognising their like in others.

debates: How should the nineteenth verse be construed? Keil and Delitzsch hold that the particle which opens it is a preposition and never a conjunction, so that the usual rendering, as in water face answereth to face, asks it to govern a whole clause; they report a conjecture that the Greek translators had a different text before them yielding faces that are not alike, and offer their own sense, that as each beholds his own face in the water so each sees his own heart in another. Henry, Ellicott and Clarke all keep the received rendering and divide over its use, for self-knowledge, for recognising one’s own temper in others, or for discerning what another is by his words and actions.
outliers: Clarke asks whether a Latin poet had read this proverb in the Greek before writing his line about the hone that sharpens iron while unable itself to cut.
Wesley alone gives the likeness of hearts a sour turn, making what one man finds in another their common corruption of nature.
Keil and Delitzsch report the Mishna’s three names for the fruit of the fig at its unripe, half ripe and fully ripe stages, in explanation of why the tree suits a proverb about long service.
Henry notes the force of the word in the eighteenth verse, that the servant keeps his master, guarding his person and reputation and seeing that his estate is not wasted.
themes: a shower one shelters from and a rain one cannot
a woman who slips through the hand like oil
the hone that cannot cut
a fig tree that pays for years of care
each man seeing his own heart in another

20.pericope_label: Hell and destruction are never full: as the fining pot for silver, so is a man to his praise: though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar, yet will not his foolishness depart from him

schools.summary: Henry makes the sepulchre cry Give, give, traces the unsatisfied eye back to the first parents who were not content with all the trees of the garden, treats praise as the assay itself so that the man who lies in bed till noon because his name is up is proved vain while the man whom praise makes more watchful is proved otherwise, and sets the fool in the mortar against the earlier proverb that the rod may drive folly out of a child while the mind is still to be moulded.

Gill proves the insatiable grave from the names given to burial places, the field called the multitude of an army, the Greek word meaning many men and the Latin usage that calls the dead simply the many, and reports where the versions place the beating of the fool, in the congregation or in the council.

Clarke feels the force of the comparison as an insult, asking how hideous the soul of a covetous man must be when God likens it to hell, and traces the changing fashions and endless modes of getting money to the same unsatisfied desire; he states the two outcomes of praise in a line, and sets aside other commentators to propose that the mortar of the twenty-second verse is taken from the pounding of metallic ores; Wesley notes that the eyes stand for the desires.

Keil and Delitzsch correct three scholars who reported a marginal reading at the twentieth verse that is not there, take the twenty-first verse of public opinion so that a man is valued by the measure of his fame as metal by the result of the smelting while reporting two scholars who make it his own glorying, and reject a proposed derivation of the word for grit; Ellicott supplies the purpose of the first proverb, that only in God can man find complete satisfaction, and offers three constructions of the second without choosing among them.

debates: What does it mean that a man is tried by his praise? Henry and Clarke make praise the fire and the man the metal, so that his behaviour under it shows what he is. Keil and Delitzsch make it a measure instead, a man being valued according to the measure of his fame as silver is valued by the result of the crucible, and report two scholars who read it of the thing in which a man places his own glory. Ellicott offers all three constructions and declines to choose, adding a fourth turn, that a man should assay his praise and see by whom and for what he is praised.
outliers: Clarke sets aside the conjectures of other commentators, of which he says they are full, and proposes that the mortar is the miner’s, used for pounding metallic ores so that fire may separate the metal.
Gill argues the insatiability of the grave from three languages, the name of a burial field, a Greek word meaning many men, and a Latin usage that calls the dead the many.
Clarke traces the changing fashions, the varied amusements and the endless modes of getting money in every age to the one unsatisfied desire of the twentieth verse.
Henry allows that some men must be dealt with roughly, by judgments and by the rigour of the law, and that with some even those methods do not answer.
themes: a grave that cries Give, give
desire behind every changing fashion
praise as the crucible
a measure of fame or of self-glorying
ore pounded and folly unseparated

23.pericope_label: Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks: for riches are not for ever: the lambs are for thy clothing, and the goats are the price of the field

schools.summary: Henry draws four rules from the command, that we ought to have some business and not live in idleness, that we ought to understand it and not meddle with what we do not understand, that we ought to have an eye to it ourselves since it is the master’s eye that makes the cattle fat, and that we ought to manage it so that nothing is lost and no opportunity let slip.

Gill notices that the Hebrew says the face of the flocks and suggests it alludes to shepherds who know each sheep distinctly, reports that the Greek read the souls of the flock as though the charge were laid on spiritual pastors, renders the hay as removed and carried off rather than appearing, and separates the he-goats sold to buy fields from the she-goats kept for a milk that physicians have ranked next to the milk of women.

Clarke tells the owner not to trust his flocks to the shepherd but to number them himself, observes that flocks properly attended to may be multiplied from generation to generation while the crown itself is not naturally so permanent, explains that the landlord is paid by the sale of lambs and goats or in fleeces, and reads the last verse at the table, where bread was eaten and milk supped together; Wesley takes flocks and herds for all possessions, since anciently they were the chief part of a man’s riches, and finds the encouragement in a provision that reaches even the barren parts of the earth.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the last five verses as a single ode of eleven lines closing a series in which they cannot always discern an intentional grouping, and translate the twenty-fifth verse with the hay gone and the after-growth appearing; Ellicott makes the same division, gives the argument that the pastoral life is set out as superior to other sources of wealth and to the regal power, and suggests the same rendering of the hay.

debates: Does the hay appear or has it gone? The English makes the hay appear at the start of the season; Ellicott suggests that it is gone instead, and Keil and Delitzsch translate so, with the after-growth following it; Gill reaches the same sense by rendering that the hay removes, being mown and carried off and laid up for the winter, after which the tender grass springs again as a second crop. Clarke passes over the question and reads the verse as instruction, that the hay be timely mown, carefully dried and safely ricked.
outliers: Gill reports that the Greek read the souls of the flock rather than its face, which turns a charge to farmers into a charge to spiritual pastors.
Clarke alone explains the economics of the last verses, that the landlord is paid either in a set number of lambs and goats or in their price, and in some places in fleeces.
Keil and Delitzsch admit that they cannot always discern an intentional grouping in the series these verses close, before identifying the verses themselves as a formal ode.
Clarke refers the reader who wants more of this husbandry to the old writers on farming, and notes that bread was eaten and milk supped together to help the chewing and swallowing.
themes: a series that ends in a poem
the master’s eye that makes cattle fat
hay appearing or hay carried off
rent paid in lambs and fleeces
a crown less permanent than a flock
